sections.title: How does the Centripetal force calculator work?
sections.html:
The Centripetal force calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mass (m) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the tangential velocity (v), the angular velocity (ω) and the centripetal acceleration (a).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second squared. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Centripetal force calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mass (m)=centripetal force (F) × radius (r) ÷ (tangential velocity (v) ^ 2)
Radius (r)=(1 ÷ 2) × tangential velocity (v) ÷ (PI × angular velocity (ω))
Mass (m)=centripetal force (F) ÷ centripetal acceleration (a)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Radius (r) = 30 m, Tangential velocity (v) = 10 m/s and Centripetal force (F) = 10 N. The calculator returns Mass (m) = 388.8 kg, Angular velocity (ω) = 1.4737 rad/s and Centripetal acceleration (a) = 25.7202 m/s².

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mass (m) = 388.8 kg, Angular velocity (ω) = 1.4737 rad/s and Centripetal acceleration (a) = 25.7202 m/s² should be roughly the size you expected from Radius (r) = 30 m and Tangential velocity (v) = 10 m/s.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in kilograms, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.
  • Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in newtons, and convertible to any of the 16 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Rotational speed, opening in radians per second
  • Force, opening in newtons
  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Centripetal force calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the tangential velocity, the angular velocity and the centripetal acceleration — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Centripetal force calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mass (m), derived from the tangential velocity, the angular velocity and the centripetal acceleration. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Centripetal force calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the tangential velocity, the angular velocity and the centripetal acceleration, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass (m) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass (m) opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mass (m) = 388.8 kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Centripetal force calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
